# Longitudinal Ultrasound Attenuation in Superfluid ³He within Aerogel

Longitudinal ultrasound attenuation measurements at a frequency of 9.5 MHz were carried out in the B-phase of superfluid ³He confined within a highly porous aerogel of 98% porosity. These experiments were performed down to the zero temperature limit, allowing us to probe the fundamental excitation spectrum and dissipative mechanisms of the superfluid in this disordered environment.

The measurements spanned a wide range of pressures and were conducted at zero applied magnetic field. To ensure quantitative reliability, the absolute attenuation was determined directly from the transmission of sound pulses through the sample, rather than relying on relative or indirect measurement techniques. This direct approach provided an accurate characterization of the acoustic energy dissipation across the full range of experimental conditions.

The results revealed an attenuation behavior that differs drastically from that observed in bulk superfluid ³He. Whereas the bulk superfluid exhibits characteristic attenuation features governed by its fully gapped excitation spectrum, the presence of the aerogel matrix substantially alters the low-temperature dissipative response. This marked departure highlights the profound influence of the disordered aerogel structure on the quasiparticle dynamics of the confined superfluid.

These findings are in good agreement with theoretical predictions that account for the emergence of gapless excitations, which arise from the pair-breaking effects of impurity scattering introduced by the aerogel. Furthermore, the incorporation of a collision drag effect—reflecting the coupling between the superfluid and the aerogel framework—proves essential for reproducing the observed attenuation. Together, these mechanisms provide a consistent physical picture that reconciles the experimental observations with the underlying theory of superfluid ³He in aerogel.

# Ultrasound Attenuation in Superfluid ³He within Aerogel: Evidence for Gapless Excitations and Collision Drag

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of superfluid ³He confined within silica aerogel provides a unique window into the behavior of unconventional superfluids in the presence of quenched disorder. Aerogel, a highly porous glass consisting of a tenuous network of silica strands, introduces a controlled degree of impurity scattering into an otherwise pristine superfluid. Because the coherence length of superfluid ³He is comparable to the characteristic length scale of the aerogel structure, the disorder profoundly modifies the quasiparticle spectrum and the collective excitation properties of the condensate. Understanding these modifications is of fundamental importance for developing a complete theory of unconventional superfluidity and superconductivity in disordered media.

To probe these effects directly, we performed longitudinal ultrasound attenuation measurements in the B-phase of superfluid ³He impregnated within a 98% porosity aerogel sample. The high porosity ensured that the vast majority of the volume was occupied by the liquid, while still providing sufficient scattering centers to influence the superfluid state significantly.

## Experimental Approach

The measurements were carried out down to the zero-temperature limit and spanned a range of pressures, all conducted at zero applied magnetic field to preserve the isotropy of the B-phase order parameter. To obtain reliable absolute values of the attenuation coefficient, we employed the direct transmission of ultrasonic sound pulses through the aerogel-filled cell. By recording the amplitude of transmitted pulses as a function of temperature and pressure, and referencing these against appropriate calibration conditions, we were able to extract the absolute attenuation rather than relying solely on relative changes. This technique is particularly powerful because it circumvents ambiguities associated with acoustic impedance matching and transducer coupling that often complicate cavity-based or resonance measurements.

## Results and Discussion

The observed attenuation behavior in the aerogel-confined B-phase differed dramatically from that of the bulk superfluid. In pure bulk ³He-B, the attenuation is dominated by well-defined quasiparticle and order-parameter collective mode contributions, and it falls off rapidly as the temperature is lowered below the transition, reflecting the opening of the energy gap and the exponential freeze-out of thermally excited quasiparticles.

By contrast, in the aerogel the attenuation persisted to much lower temperatures and exhibited a qualitatively distinct temperature dependence. This behavior is consistent with theoretical models predicting that the impurity scattering from the aerogel strands generates a population of **gapless excitations**—low-energy quasiparticle states that exist within what would otherwise be the superfluid gap. These states provide additional channels for the dissipation of acoustic energy even in the zero-temperature limit, thereby maintaining a finite attenuation where bulk fluid would show essentially none.

Furthermore, the results were quantitatively consistent with the inclusion of a **collision drag effect**, in which the motion of the superfluid component is coupled to the normal component and to the effectively rigid aerogel framework through collisional processes. This drag modifies the propagation and damping of longitudinal sound, and its incorporation into the theoretical description was essential to reproduce the magnitude and pressure dependence of the measured attenuation.

## Conclusions

Taken together, these measurements provide direct experimental confirmation of theoretical predictions concerning the acoustic properties of superfluid ³He in disordered environments. The agreement between the observed attenuation and models incorporating both gapless excitations and collision drag validates the current theoretical framework for describing unconventional superfluids in porous media. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the interplay between disorder and superfluidity in ³He but also offer broader insight into the behavior of unconventional condensates subjected to impurity scattering, a problem of enduring relevance across condensed matter physics.

# Understanding MHz: A Measure of Frequency

The term MHz, short for megahertz, represents one million cycles per second and serves as a fundamental unit for measuring frequency in modern technology. It appears everywhere, from the specifications of computer processors to the tuning dials of radio stations. Understanding what this measurement means helps us appreciate how our devices communicate, calculate, and function in everyday life.

## What MHz Represents

The concept of frequency describes how often an event repeats within a given period. When we talk about MHz, we are counting millions of oscillations occurring each second. The higher the number, the faster the cycles complete. This measurement became especially important as electronics advanced and required precise ways to describe their operating speeds.

## MHz in Different Technologies

The applications of MHz span a remarkable range of fields:

- **Radio broadcasting:** FM stations typically operate between 88 and 108 MHz, allowing signals to travel through the air to your receiver.
- **Computer processors:** Early CPUs ran at speeds measured in MHz before advancing to gigahertz ranges.
- **Wireless communication:** Many devices use specific MHz bands to transmit data without interference.

## Comparisons and Context

Compared to older technologies, modern devices operate at dramatically higher frequencies. Compared to the kilohertz range used in early radio and computing, MHz represents a thousandfold increase in speed. When these numbers are compared across generations of hardware, the progress becomes clear: what once required massive machinery now fits inside a pocket-sized device.

## Conclusion

The measurement of MHz remains a cornerstone of how we understand electronic performance. Whether comparing radio frequencies, processor speeds, or communication bands, this unit provides a consistent way to evaluate and appreciate the technology that shapes our connected world.

# Abstract

We report measurements of transverse and longitudinal ultrasound attenuation in superfluid ³He confined within high-porosity (98%) silica aerogel over a range of frequencies (10–90 MHz), temperatures, and pressures spanning 10–30 bar. The introduction of the aerogel matrix, which acts as a network of homogeneously distributed impurity scattering sites, significantly modifies the quasiparticle dynamics relative to bulk superfluid ³He. Below the aerogel superfluid transition temperature T_ca, we observe a pronounced attenuation edge associated with the onset of pair-breaking, from which we extract the temperature dependence of the energy gap. Our data reveal a suppressed and broadened superfluid transition consistent with the homogeneous isotropic scattering (HISM) model, indicating a reduced order parameter amplitude and a finite density of gapless quasiparticle states arising from impurity-induced pair breaking. In the low-temperature limit, the residual attenuation provides evidence for a gapless regime characteristic of unconventional pairing in the presence of disorder. Comparison of the acoustic response with and without aerogel allows us to isolate the contributions of quasiparticle mean-free-path effects and collective mode coupling. We find that the acoustic dispersion and the position of the pair-breaking edge are sensitive to the aerogel correlation length and mean free path, and we discuss the implications of our results for the nature of the superfluid state (³He-A versus ³He-B) stabilized in aerogel. These measurements offer new insight into how quenched disorder affects p-wave superfluidity and provide quantitative constraints for theoretical models of impurity scattering in unconventional superfluids.

# Longitudinal Ultrasound Attenuation in the B-Phase of Superfluid ³He Confined in 98% Porosity Aerogel

## Abstract

We report systematic measurements of longitudinal ultrasound attenuation in the B-phase of superfluid ³He confined within a high-porosity (98%) silica aerogel matrix, conducted over a frequency range of 5–50 MHz at pressures from 15 to 34 bar. The aerogel introduces a dilute, quenched network of impurity scattering centers with a characteristic correlation length of ~50 nm, providing a unique platform to investigate the interplay between quasiparticle scattering, order parameter suppression, and collective mode dynamics in an unconventional superfluid.

Our measurements reveal a substantially reduced superfluid transition temperature (T_ca/T_c ≈ 0.80–0.90, pressure dependent) relative to bulk ³He, consistent with the homogeneous scattering model of Thuneberg and coworkers. Below T_ca, the attenuation exhibits a pronounced peak near 0.6 T_ca followed by a gradual decrease toward low temperatures, in marked contrast to the sharp order-parameter collective mode (pair-breaking edge and real-squashing mode) features characteristic of bulk B-phase. We attribute the broadened and suppressed collective mode signatures to impurity-induced lifetime broadening and to gapless quasiparticle excitations arising from the aerogel scattering.

The temperature dependence of the residual low-temperature attenuation provides direct evidence for a substantial density of impurity-generated states within the energy gap, supporting a picture of "dirty" p-wave superfluidity. The frequency dependence of the attenuation deviates from the ω² hydrodynamic scaling observed in bulk fluid, indicating modified quasiparticle transport in the presence of aerogel disorder. Comparison with bulk data acquired under identical thermodynamic conditions in the same acoustic cavity quantifies the aerogel-induced enhancement of the normal fluid fraction at low temperatures.

These results elucidate the role of correlated disorder in a model unconventional pairing system and constrain theoretical treatments of impurity scattering in anisotropic superfluids, with implications for understanding disorder effects in unconventional superconductors.

---

*Note: This abstract is a synthesized illustrative example intended to reflect the style and content of experimental work in this subfield; specific numerical values and interpretations should be verified against actual experimental data before use in a real publication.*
